questions.stem:
A 42-year-old man had a flu-like illness that over several weeks progressed to worsening shortness of breath. A lung biopsy is examined. Giemsa and silver stains show large round yeast forms, several of which have a single daughter cell attached across a wide, flat connection to the parent cell. No hyphae are seen.

Which organism produces this appearance?
choices: Cryptococcus neoformans
Blastomyces dermatitidis
Coccidioides immitis spherules
Aspergillus niger
Histoplasma capsulatum
questions.note:
**Large yeast with a single broad-based bud in lung tissue identifies Blastomyces dermatitidis.**

Large yeast with a single bud attached across a broad base is the characteristic tissue form of Blastomyces dermatitidis. Infection follows inhalation of spores and primarily involves the lung, where it can produce an indolent or progressive pneumonia.

The width of the attachment is the discriminating detail: Cryptococcus buds on a narrow base and is encapsulated, and Histoplasma is small and lives inside macrophages.

Cryptococcus neoformans: incorrect. Cryptococcus has narrow-based budding and a thick capsule.

Blastomyces dermatitidis: correct. Broad-based budding yeast is Blastomyces dermatitidis.

Coccidioides immitis spherules: incorrect. Coccidioides forms thick-walled spherules filled with endospores, not budding yeast.

Aspergillus niger: incorrect. Aspergillus is a mold with septate hyphae, not a budding yeast.

Histoplasma capsulatum: incorrect. Histoplasma yeast is small and found within macrophages.

questions.stem:
A pathology laboratory processes four specimens from different patients. For specimen 1 a silver stain of lung tissue outlines fungal walls in dark brown against a pale background. For specimen 2 a drop of cerebrospinal fluid is mixed with a particulate ink and examined wet. Specimen 3 is a bone marrow aspirate stained with a Romanowsky-type stain. Specimen 4 is a skin biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff.

Which statement about these methods is correct?
choices: The particulate ink stains the organism itself a dark color
The silver method outlines fungal walls in tissue
The marrow stain cannot show organisms inside phagocytes
Periodic acid-Schiff stains only bacterial peptidoglycan
All four methods require viable organisms to be useful
questions.note:
**Silver and periodic acid-Schiff stains show fungal walls in tissue, India ink is a negative stain for capsule, and Wright-Giemsa shows yeast inside phagocytes.**

These are the staining methods used across the case set. Silver stains outline fungal cell walls and are the standard way to find fungi in tissue sections, including both yeast and hyphal forms.

India ink is a negative stain: the ink particles cannot enter the capsule, so the organism and its capsule appear light against a dark background. Romanowsky-type stains such as Wright-Giemsa show organisms inside phagocytes on marrow and blood films, and periodic acid-Schiff highlights fungal wall carbohydrate in tissue.

The particulate ink stains the organism itself a dark color: incorrect. India ink is a negative stain; the organism is not darkened by it.

The silver method outlines fungal walls in tissue: correct. Silver methods outline fungal cell walls and are the standard tissue stain for fungi.

The marrow stain cannot show organisms inside phagocytes: incorrect. Wright-Giemsa is exactly how intracellular yeast forms are seen on a marrow aspirate.

Periodic acid-Schiff stains only bacterial peptidoglycan: incorrect. Periodic acid-Schiff highlights carbohydrate in fungal walls, not bacterial peptidoglycan.

All four methods require viable organisms to be useful: incorrect. These are morphologic stains and do not require living organisms.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma recently treated with combination chemotherapy has fever, severe headaches, and new seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid is obtained. A Giemsa-stained preparation shows round cells of varying size with narrow-based budding, and an India ink preparation of the same fluid shows a wide unstained zone surrounding each cell.

Which morphologic feature in this preparation most directly establishes the diagnosis?
choices: Clusters of small cells inside leukocytes
Thick-walled structures packed with endospores
Hyphae with regular cross walls
The wide unstained zone around each cell
A single bud attached across a wide base
questions.note:
**A clear halo on India ink preparation of cerebrospinal fluid represents the cryptococcal capsule and identifies Cryptococcus in an immunocompromised host.**

India ink is a negative stain: the particles cannot enter the thick polysaccharide capsule, so the capsule appears as a clear halo around the yeast. Combined with narrow-based budding and a central nervous system presentation in an immunocompromised patient, this identifies Cryptococcus.

The other morphologies on this slide set point elsewhere, which is the skill being tested: match what is seen under the microscope to the organism and then to the clinical picture.

Clusters of small cells inside leukocytes: incorrect. Small cells packed inside phagocytes describe Histoplasma.

Thick-walled structures packed with endospores: incorrect. Thick-walled structures filled with endospores are Coccidioides spherules.

Hyphae with regular cross walls: incorrect. Septate hyphae indicate a mold such as Aspergillus, not a yeast in cerebrospinal fluid.

The wide unstained zone around each cell: correct. The clear halo on India ink is the cryptococcal capsule.

A single bud attached across a wide base: incorrect. Broad-based budding describes Blastomyces, which does not typically present this way.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old missionary recently back from Central America has fever, weight loss, pancytopenia, and altered mental status, with an enlarged liver and spleen. A Wright-Giemsa stained bone marrow aspirate shows many small oval cells clustered inside mononuclear cells, and a silver stain of the same aspirate highlights the same small forms.

These findings are most consistent with which organism?
choices: Sporothrix schenckii
Rhizopus species
Blastomyces species
Aspergillus fumigatus
Histoplasma capsulatum
questions.note:
**Small yeast forms within macrophages on a bone marrow aspirate, with pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, indicate disseminated histoplasmosis.**

Small oval yeast forms packed inside mononuclear phagocytes on a bone marrow aspirate, in a patient with fever, weight loss, pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, are the hallmark of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus that survives and multiplies inside macrophages, which is why marrow, liver and spleen are involved and why the peripheral counts fall.

Sporothrix schenckii: incorrect. Sporothrix produces lymphocutaneous lesions after skin inoculation.

Rhizopus species: incorrect. Rhizopus forms broad aseptate hyphae in tissue.

Blastomyces species: incorrect. Blastomyces is a large yeast with broad-based budding, not a small intracellular form.

Aspergillus fumigatus: incorrect. Aspergillus is a mold with septate hyphae and does not reside inside macrophages.

Histoplasma capsulatum: correct. Small yeast forms multiplying within macrophages are Histoplasma.

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a rapidly developing facial lesion involving the nose and cheek, with dark discolored dead tissue at its center. A biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff shows broad, irregular, ribbon-like hyphae that lack cross walls and branch at wide angles. The lesion has expanded noticeably over 48 hours.

Which feature of the biopsy best distinguishes this organism from the other common mold causing invasive disease?
choices: Absence of septa and wide-angle branching
Presence of budding yeast alongside the hyphae
A thick capsule surrounding each hypha
Arthrospores forming along the filaments
Pigmented granules within the tissue
questions.note:
**Broad aseptate ribbon-like hyphae branching at wide angles identify mucormycosis and distinguish it from septate, acute-angle Aspergillus.**

A rapidly progressive facial infection with necrotic tissue in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes is mucormycosis. On histology the agents of mucormycosis form broad, irregular, ribbon-like hyphae with no septa that branch at roughly right angles.

Aspergillus, the other common invasive mold, is the look-alike: its hyphae are narrower, regularly septate, and branch at acute angles. Separating them on biopsy matters because the management differs.

**Mucormycosis agents | Aspergillus**

- Septa: Absent; Present
- Branching: Wide (right) angles; Acute (45 degree) angles
- Hyphal shape: Broad, ribbon-like, irregular; Narrow, uniform

Absence of septa and wide-angle branching: correct. Aseptate ribbon-like hyphae branching at wide angles separate the agents of mucormycosis from Aspergillus.

Presence of budding yeast alongside the hyphae: incorrect. Budding yeast beside hyphae suggests Candida, not a mold invading tissue.

A thick capsule surrounding each hypha: incorrect. Hyphae are not encapsulated; a capsule is a feature of Cryptococcus yeast.

Arthrospores forming along the filaments: incorrect. Arthrospores form in soil cultures of Coccidioides, not in this tissue.

Pigmented granules within the tissue: incorrect. Pigmented granules are not the distinguishing feature here.

questions.stem:
A previously healthy 35-year-old woman has low-grade fever, cough, and chest pain. A chest radiograph shows a single nodule in the left upper lobe. Her symptoms began about 3 weeks after she returned from a trip through the Sonoran Desert. Lung biopsy stained with hematoxylin and eosin and with silver shows large round thick-walled structures, some containing many small round bodies inside them.

How is this organism acquired?
choices: Contact with pigeon droppings during demolition
Spread along lymphatics from a distant abscess
Inhalation of arthrospores from dry soil
Ingestion of contaminated water
Inoculation of the organism into a skin wound
questions.note:
**Spherules filled with endospores in lung tissue identify Coccidioides, acquired by inhaling arthrospores from dry desert soil.**

Thick-walled structures filled with small internal bodies are spherules containing endospores, the tissue form of Coccidioides, and the Sonoran Desert travel history fits the endemic area of the southwestern United States.

In soil the organism grows as filaments that reproduce by forming arthrospores, which become airborne when dry alkaline soil is disturbed and are inhaled. A solitary nodule weeks after exposure is a typical primary pulmonary presentation.

Contact with pigeon droppings during demolition: incorrect. Pigeon droppings are linked to Cryptococcus neoformans.

Spread along lymphatics from a distant abscess: incorrect. Lymphatic spread from an abscess does not describe primary pulmonary infection.

Inhalation of arthrospores from dry soil: correct. Coccidioides is acquired by inhaling arthrospores from dry desert soil.

Ingestion of contaminated water: incorrect. Waterborne ingestion is not how this organism is acquired.

Inoculation of the organism into a skin wound: incorrect. Skin inoculation describes sporotrichosis and mycetoma.

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man with multiple risk factors for immunosuppression has increasing difficulty swallowing with pain on swallowing. Endoscopy shows white plaques lining the esophagus, and his tongue is coated with similar white material that can be scraped off. A biopsy stained with periodic acid-Schiff shows budding yeast together with elongated chains of cells that remain attached end to end.

The elongated attached chains in this biopsy are best described as which structure?
choices: Pseudohyphae formed by budding yeast cells
Arthrospores released from filaments
Endospores escaping a spherule
Sporangiospores held within a sac
Septate true hyphae of a mold
questions.note:
**Budding yeast with pseudohyphae on a mucosal biopsy identifies Candida as the cause of thrush and esophagitis.**

White plaques on the tongue and esophagus with budding yeast on biopsy indicate candidiasis. Candida forms pseudohyphae, which are chains of elongated budding cells that stay attached rather than true hyphae with continuous cytoplasm.

Recognizing budding yeast with pseudohyphae on a mucosal biopsy is the morphologic step that distinguishes Candida from the molds and from the dimorphic fungi in tissue.

Pseudohyphae formed by budding yeast cells: correct. Chains of elongated budding cells that remain attached are pseudohyphae, typical of Candida.

Arthrospores released from filaments: incorrect. Arthrospores are formed in soil by Coccidioides filaments.

Endospores escaping a spherule: incorrect. Endospores come from Coccidioides spherules in tissue.

Sporangiospores held within a sac: incorrect. Sporangiospores are spores contained within a sporangium, not seen here.

Septate true hyphae of a mold: incorrect. True septate hyphae belong to molds such as Aspergillus.

questions.stem:
Two patients with hematologic disease develop pulmonary infiltrates. Patient 1 has been profoundly neutropenic for 3 weeks after induction chemotherapy and has hemoptysis; biopsy shows narrow hyphae with regular cross walls branching at acute angles, invading vessel walls. Patient 2 has lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and presents with headache and seizures; the cerebrospinal fluid shows round cells with a wide clear zone on a negative stain.

Which pairing of host defect to organism is correct?
choices: Both infections follow inhalation of arthrospores from desert soil
Neither organism requires an immune defect to invade tissue
Neutropenia with Cryptococcus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Aspergillus
Neutropenia with Aspergillus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Cryptococcus
Both infections are explained by loss of the skin barrier
questions.note:
**Invasive aspergillosis follows prolonged neutropenia, while disseminated cryptococcosis follows impaired cell-mediated immunity.**

Septate hyphae branching at acute angles that invade vessels in a profoundly neutropenic patient are invasive aspergillosis; prolonged, profound neutropenia is the classic setting.

Round cells with a wide clear zone on a negative stain in cerebrospinal fluid are encapsulated Cryptococcus, which disseminates to the central nervous system when cell-mediated immunity fails, as in lymphoma treated with chemotherapy or in advanced human immunodeficiency virus infection.

Both infections follow inhalation of arthrospores from desert soil: incorrect. Arthrospores from desert soil are the route for Coccidioides.

Neither organism requires an immune defect to invade tissue: incorrect. Both organisms cause invasive disease mainly in impaired hosts.

Neutropenia with Cryptococcus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Aspergillus: incorrect. This reverses the two host defects.

Neutropenia with Aspergillus, impaired cell-mediated immunity with Cryptococcus: correct. Neutropenia predisposes to invasive Aspergillus, while impaired cell-mediated immunity predisposes to disseminated Cryptococcus.

Both infections are explained by loss of the skin barrier: incorrect. Neither infection began at a skin wound; both followed inhalation.
